questions.explanation: Correct Answer: D. Educational Objective: The most appropriate next step for this patient is recommendation for low back exercises. Acute to subacute low back pain with radicular symptoms but no neurologic deficits or red flags should be initially managed conservatively with activity modification and exercise. Evaluation: This patient has low back pain radiating down the posterior leg with a positive straight-leg raise test, consistent with lumbar radiculopathy, but has no weakness, sensory deficits, or bowel or bladder dysfunction, indicating no red flags. Definition: Lumbar radiculopathy is most commonly caused by intervertebral disc herniation leading to nerve root compression, often presenting with radiating pain along a dermatomal distribution. Most cases improve spontaneously within 6 to 12 weeks, and initial management is conservative. Imaging such as MRI is reserved for patients with red flag symptoms including progressive neurologic deficits, cauda equina syndrome, or persistent symptoms beyond approximately 6 weeks that fail conservative therapy. Early imaging does not improve outcomes and may lead to unnecessary interventions. Prevention: Regular core strengthening and proper lifting techniques decrease risk for recurrent low back pain. Treatment: First-line treatment includes NSAIDs and maintenance of activity with targeted exercises to strengthen the back and improve function. Differential: Muscle strain presents with localized back pain without radicular symptoms and typically has a negative straight-leg raise test. Spinal stenosis causes neurogenic claudication with pain worsened by walking and relieved by flexion, rather than acute radicular pain. Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, E, and F. Choice A: Electromyography and nerve conduction studies is incorrect. These are used in chronic or unclear cases and are not part of initial management. Choice B: Laminectomy is incorrect. Surgical intervention is reserved for severe or refractory cases with neurologic deficits or failure of conservative therapy. Choice C: MRI of the spine is incorrect. Imaging is not indicated initially in the absence of red flag symptoms and should be deferred unless symptoms persist beyond approximately 6 weeks or worsen. Choice E: Use of a back brace is incorrect. Bracing does not improve outcomes and may contribute to muscle deconditioning, worsening the long-term outcome. Choice F: X-rays of the lumbosacral spine is incorrect. Plain x-rays are not useful in evaluating radiculopathy and are not indicated without suspicion for fracture or malignancy.

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: A. Educational Objective: This patient presents with a 3-cm reducible umbilical hernia. The most likely clinical course of her current condition is complete resolution after surgical repair. Evaluation: An umbilical hernia may present with a soft, reducible bulge at the umbilicus that may become more prominent with straining or coughing. Definition: An umbilical hernia occurs due to failure of spontaneous closure of the umbilical ring. Following birth, the umbilical ring is progressively closed by the rectus abdominis muscles and is accompanied by fusion of the muscular fascial layers and of the peritoneal membrane. Complete closure occurs in most children during infancy. Prevention: There is no known way to prevent the development of an umbilical hernia. Treatment: The majority of children with an umbilical hernia experience spontaneous resolution by age 3 years. Children with large defects (greater than 1.5 cm) or persistent defects are less likely to experience spontaneous closure and may undergo progressive enlargement of the defect over time. A minority of patients with persistent defects or who develop intestinal incarceration may require surgical intervention. Differential: This patient presents with a large persistent umbilical hernia. Complete resolution after surgical repair can be expected. Incorrect Answers: B, C, and D. Choice B: Incarceration of the large intestine is incorrect. This patient has a reducible umbilical hernia. Large intestine incarceration in cases of umbilical hernias is fairly uncommon. Complete resolution after surgical repair is more likely. Choice C: Incarceration of the small intestine is incorrect. Incarceration of the small intestine is a rare complication of an umbilical hernia. Complete resolution after surgical repair is the more likely clinical course in this case. Choice D: Spontaneous resolution by adolescence is incorrect. Spontaneous closure of an umbilical hernia becomes less likely after age 4 to 5 years. Complete resolution after surgical repair is more likely.

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: F. Educational Objective: In an adult patient with capacity, their permission must be obtained prior to sharing health care information; therefore, the most appropriate response to the woman's request is to inform the woman that the patient's medical information cannot be shared without his permission. Key Concept: HIPAA protects patient health information (PHI) and prevents dissemination of PHI without consent. Explanation: Patients have a right to privacy, protected by HIPAA. In this case, where the patient is alert and demonstrates decisional capacity, PHI cannot be provided to the patient’s mother without his permission. Differential: Patients maintain a right to privacy, and PHI cannot be shared with others without permission. Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, and E. Choice A: Ask the woman if she is aware of the patient's insurance status is incorrect. The patient has a right to privacy, including his health insurance information status. In this case no information can be shared without his consent. Choice B: Ask the woman to complete a health care proxy form if she would like to receive updates on the patient's condition is incorrect. In this case the patient retains capacity and a right to privacy. He may determine if he would like to share information with others, in addition to determining his health care proxy. Choice C: Ask the woman to confirm the patient's social security number before providing any information is incorrect. A social security number represents PHI and should not be discussed with the person on the phone. The patient’s consent is required before any information regarding his health is shared. Choice D and Choice E: Inform the woman that the patient was in a motorcycle collision and may have been under the influence of alcohol and/or drugs and inform the woman that the patient's condition is stable and that x-rays have been ordered are incorrect. The patient has the right to privacy, based on HIPAA policies. No information should be shared with the woman without the patient’s permission.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man is brought to the emergency department (ED) 20 minutes after a motorcycle collision in which he crashed into an embankment at an unknown rate of speed and was thrown 20 feet. The patient was wearing a helmet and did not lose consciousness. He landed on his right side and reports severe pain in his right arm and shoulder. He notes no other pain or symptoms. Medical history is unremarkable and he takes no medications. He has smoked 5 to 10 cigarettes daily for 4 years and he drinks one to two alcoholic beverages daily. He smokes marijuana two to three times weekly and occasionally uses methamphetamine. The patient appears uncomfortable but is alert and interactive. Temperature is 37.2°C (98.9°F), pulse is 122/min and regular, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 144/86 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on oxygen at 2 L/min via nasal cannula shows an oxygen saturation of 96%. Examination of the extremities shows an obvious deformity of the right proximal humerus without skin laceration or trauma. Sensation to light touch is intact and capillary refill time is brisk in all extremities. X-rays of the chest, right shoulder, and right upper extremity are ordered. During the patient's initial evaluation, a woman calls the ED, identifies herself as the patient's mother, and asks about his condition. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in response to the woman's request?

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: B. Educational Objective: Primary ovarian insufficiency (POI) is characterized by amenorrhea, hypoestrogenism, and increased gonadotropin concentrations in women younger than 40 years. Continuous oral contraceptives are a mainstay of treatment to manage symptoms and prevent long-term complications. Key Concept: POI typically presents with secondary amenorrhea, vasomotor symptoms (eg, hot flashes, night sweats), and infertility. Laboratory studies show increased follicle-stimulating hormone and decreased estradiol concentrations, with normal thyroid function and prolactin concentrations. Explanation: POI results from loss of ovarian function before age 40 years, leading to decreased estrogen production and increased gonadotropin concentrations. Causes include autoimmune disorders, genetic abnormalities (eg, Turner syndrome), iatrogenic damage (eg, surgery, chemotherapy, radiation), and idiopathic disease. Hypoestrogenism can cause vasomotor symptoms, vaginal atrophy, and increased risk for osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease. Management focuses on hormone replacement therapy, such as continuous or cyclic oral contraceptives, to alleviate symptoms, maintain bone density, and decrease long-term cardiovascular effects of estrogen deficiency. Differential: In this 23-year-old patient with amenorrhea, hot flashes, and increased follicle-stimulating hormone, POI is the most likely diagnosis. Estrogen replacement with continuous oral contraceptive is indicated. Her age and laboratory findings differentiate premature ovarian failure from normal menopause or other causes of amenorrhea. Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E. Choice A: Androgen replacement is incorrect. Androgen therapy is not first-line for hypoestrogenism and does not address hot flashes or bone loss associated with POI. Choice C: Fluoxetine is incorrect. Although fluoxetine and other selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors can improve vasomotor symptoms, estrogen replacement is preferred in young women with POI because it treats the underlying hypoestrogenism. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors do not address hormonal deficiency or its long-term complications. Choice D: Gabapentin is incorrect. While gabapentin can improve vasomotor symptoms, it does not treat the underlying hypoestrogenism or prevent long-term complications like osteoporosis. Choice E: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone analog is incorrect. Gonadotropin-releasing hormone analogs suppress ovarian function and decrease estrogen production. They do not restore estrogen in patients with POI.

Educational Objective: This patient presents for routine examination with increased risk factors for coronary atherosclerosis, including cigarette smoking history, increased BMI, and hypertension. The most appropriate next step is to check serum lipid studies to further characterize atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk. Evaluation: Coronary atherosclerosis can be asymptomatic until patients develop hemodynamically significant disease, which can present with angina. The gold standard for diagnosis of hyperlipidemia is serum lipid studies. Lipid panel screening is currently recommended starting at age 19 years and repeated at least every 5 years, with more frequent screening for those with additional atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk factors. Definition: Coronary atherosclerosis results from the accumulation of apolipoprotein B–containing lipoproteins that become retained in the subintimal arterial wall, triggering maladaptive inflammatory processes and initiating atheroma formation. Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease can develop in patients with risk factors or genetic predisposition and can be mitigated by optimal lipid control. Prevention: Coronary atherosclerosis and hyperlipidemia can be prevented with lifestyle modification and medication management of risk factors. In patients with hyperlipidemia, initiation of lipid-lowering therapy can decrease the lipid profile toward the normal range and mitigate coronary risk. Treatment: Treatment for hyperlipidemia includes statin therapy and adjunctive lipid-lowering medications such as ezetimibe and proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) inhibitors. Differential: This patient's differential is initially broad, as she presents for a routine examination. However, further history shows multiple risk factors for coronary artery disease, including heavy smoking history, BMI of 35 kg/m2, increased blood pressure of 135/90 mm Hg, and absent pedal pulses, raising concern for vascular disease. Given the high pretest probability of hyperlipidemia and the need to quantify atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk, serum lipid studies are the most appropriate next step. Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E. Choice A: Exercise stress test is incorrect. Exercise stress testing is not recommended for asymptomatic patients without known coronary artery disease. Choice B: Measurement of serum C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration is incorrect. While CRP testing could be considered as a risk-enhancing marker, it is not the most appropriate next step. Serum lipid studies are more appropriate and align with public health screening guidelines. Choice D: X-ray of the chest is incorrect. Chest x-ray is used for patients who present with acute chest pain to evaluate for cardiopulmonary conditions. This patient has no chest pain, and a chest x-ray would not be appropriate. Choice E: Carotid duplex ultrasonography is incorrect. Carotid duplex ultrasonography is used to evaluate carotid stenosis in patients with a history of cerebral ischemia or a carotid bruit on examination, neither of which this patient has. While it could be considered given her multiple atherosclerotic risk factors, serum lipid studies remain the most appropriate next step.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman comes to the physician for a routine examination. She has had no recent illness and takes no medications. She walks 1 to 2 miles without having discomfort or fatigue. She smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years but quit 6 months ago. She is 152 cm (5 ft) tall and weighs 82 kg (180 lb); BMI is 35 kg/m2. Her pulse is 64/min and regular, and blood pressure is 135/90 mm Hg. Pedal pulses are absent. Capillary refill time is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: B. Educational Objective: This patient’s noncontraceptive concerns would most successfully be treated with combined hormonal contraceptives, such as the combination contraceptive patch, which decrease menstrual blood loss and are an effective treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding. Key Concept: Heavy menstrual bleeding may present with passage of clots and symptoms of anemia, such as fatigue or decreased hemoglobin concentrations. In reproductive-age women with normal pelvic examinations, hormonal causes are common and can be managed medically. Explanation: Heavy menstrual bleeding refers to excessive menstrual bleeding that interferes with quality of life and may lead to anemia. Causes include hormonal imbalance, leiomyomata uteri, and bleeding disorders, among others. Combined hormonal contraceptives stabilize the endometrium and decrease endometrial proliferation, resulting in lighter, more predictable menses. They also decrease prostaglandin production, which can improve dysmenorrhea. These effects make combined hormonal contraceptives a first-line treatment option for patients seeking both cycle control and symptom relief. Differential: In this reproductive-age patient with heavy menstrual bleeding, passage of clots, and anemia, a combined hormonal contraceptive, such as the combined contraceptive patch, addresses both contraception and bleeding control. Nonhormonal contraceptive methods would not improve her symptoms. Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E. Choices A, D, and E: Cervical cap, diaphragm, and spermicidal foam and condoms are incorrect. These are all nonhormonal barrier contraceptive methods that have no effect on heavy menstrual bleeding or dysmenorrhea. Choice C: Copper IUD is incorrect. Copper IUDs commonly increase menstrual bleeding and cramping, which would worsen this patient’s symptoms.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician requesting advice regarding contraception. Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals. During the past year, she has had an increasingly heavy menstrual flow with moderate cramping and passage of clots. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She is sexually active with one male partner. Examination shows no abnormalities. Her hemoglobin concentration is 10 g/dL. Which of the following contraceptive methods will most successfully treat this patient's noncontraceptive concerns?

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: D. Educational Objective: This patient presents with fever and a painful, erythematous, palpable cord in his forearm with enlarged epitrochlear lymph nodes. This presentation is most consistent with septic thrombophlebitis, likely following intravenous (IV) antibiotic therapy for pneumonia. Evaluation: Septic thrombophlebitis classically presents with fever and local findings over an affected vein, such as an erythematous palpable cord. The gold standard for diagnosis of septic thrombophlebitis is with clinical examination, positive blood cultures notable for persistent bacteremia, and duplex ultrasonography for diagnosis and assessment of thrombus extent. Definition: It results from catheter insertion damaging the vascular endothelium, initiating an inflammatory response and thrombus formation, followed by bacterial colonization of the thrombus that creates an infectious nidus. Prevention: Septic thrombophlebitis can be prevented by avoiding overly frequent replacement of peripheral IV catheters, as repeated insertions increase the risk for vascular endothelial damage. Peripheral IV catheters should be exchanged every 72 to 96 hours in adults. Treatment: Treatment for septic thrombophlebitis includes broad-spectrum antibiotics covering Staphylococcus aureus for a minimum duration of 3 to 4 weeks, catheter removal, and consideration of anticoagulation to treat the thrombus depending on its location. Differential: The presence of a fever, erythematous palpable cord in the forearm at the likely site of prior IV catheter insertion, and recent IV antibiotic therapy is most consistent with septic thrombophlebitis. Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E. Choice A: Cellulitis is incorrect. Cellulitis is an infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue and would not account for the palpable cord in the forearm that is consistent with venous involvement in this patient. Choice B: Deep venous thrombosis is incorrect. While deep venous thrombosis can produce a palpable cord, it would involve a deep vein rather than a superficial vein such as the one at the site of prior IV catheter insertion in this patient's forearm. Choice C: Lymphangitis is incorrect. Lymphangitis is inflammation of the lymphatic vessels and would not account for the vascular cord and infectious findings consistent with septic thrombophlebitis in this patient. Choice E: Thromboangiitis obliterans is incorrect. Thromboangiitis obliterans is an inflammatory condition affecting the small and medium vessels of the hands and feet and is strongly associated with tobacco use. This patient’s presentation is most consistent with septic thrombophlebitis.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of fever and mild pain in his right forearm. Three days ago, he was discharged from the hospital after receiving intravenous antibiotic therapy for pneumonia. On arrival, his temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 146/78 mm Hg. Examination of the right upper extremity shows erythema and a palpable cord in the forearm; there is no exudate. Two epitrochlear lymph nodes are enlarged. The lungs are clear to auscultation on the right, and a few basilar crackles are heard on the left. Cardiac examination shows no S3 or murmurs. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: A. Educational Objective: In pregnant patients with significant vaginal bleeding but stable maternal vital signs and reassuring fetal status, such as this patient, the initial step is continuous maternal-fetal monitoring. Immediate delivery is not indicated unless there is maternal instability or nonreassuring fetal status. Key Concept: Second- or third-trimester vaginal bleeding requires rapid assessment of both maternal and fetal stability. A normal fetal heart rate with moderate variability indicates reassuring fetal status, guiding initial management. Explanation: Antepartum hemorrhage refers to bleeding after 20 weeks’ gestation and includes causes such as placenta previa and abruptio placentae. Initial management focuses on stabilization and assessment of fetal status rather than immediate delivery prior to establishing fetal status. Continuous fetal monitoring helps detect early signs of fetal distress, which would necessitate urgent intervention. In cases where fetal status is reassuring, expectant management and further diagnostic evaluation are appropriate if bleeding slows and maternal stability also improves or is maintained. Premature delivery carries significant neonatal risks, especially at 26 weeks’ gestation. Differential: This patient in the second trimester has heavy bleeding but a reassuring fetal heart tracing, making monitoring the most appropriate immediate step. Her stable blood pressure and normal fetal variability argue against the need for emergent delivery. Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E. Choice B: Administration of oxytocin is incorrect. Oxytocin is used to induce or to augment labor. This patient does not yet have an emergent indication for delivery, making oxytocin use premature. Further, depending on her cause of vaginal bleeding, vaginal delivery may not be appropriate (eg, in cases of placenta previa). Choice C: Administration of a prostaglandin is incorrect. Prostaglandins are used for cervical ripening and for labor induction, among other uses. This patient has antepartum bleeding, and it is not yet clear whether she requires emergent delivery. Choice D: Artificial rupture of membranes is incorrect. Artificial rupture of membranes is used to induce labor. This patient has antepartum bleeding from an unclear source. If her cause is placenta previa, instrumentation around the cervix could result in life-threatening hemorrhage. Further, it is not yet known if she requires labor induction, as initial fetal monitoring suggests a stable fetus. Choice E: Cesarean delivery is incorrect. Cesarean delivery is used to deliver a fetus in cases where vaginal delivery is dangerous or impossible, or in cases of maternal or fetal distress, among other indications. It is not yet clear whether this patient’s fetus is immediately threatened, and the source of vaginal bleeding is not yet known. Further assessment is appropriate prior to operative management.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by paramedics after her neighbor found her lying in the hallway incoherent and bleeding heavily from the vagina. She is unable to provide her medical history. Her pulse is 135/min, respirations are 23/min, and blood pressure is 130/85 mm Hg. Physical examination shows mild, diffuse abdominal tenderness. External fetal monitoring shows a heart rate of 130/min with moderate variability. Examination shows heavy vaginal bleeding. Ultrasonography shows a uterus consistent in size with a 26-week gestation. Intravenous access is established, and blood is drawn for laboratory studies. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: E. Educational Objective: This patient with a lifelong history of easy bruising and excessive bleeding after dental procedures without hemarthroses, along with normal platelet count, most likely has von Willebrand disease. Von Willebrand disease presents with mucocutaneous bleeding and normal platelet count and is confirmed with a ristocetin cofactor assay showing impaired platelet adhesion. Evaluation: Patients with von Willebrand disease present with mucocutaneous bleeding such as epistaxis, gingival bleeding, and easy bruising, rather than deep tissue bleeding. Laboratory findings typically show normal platelet count and may show prolonged bleeding time, with variable effects on partial thromboplastin time depending on factor VIII (antihemophilic factor) concentrations. The ristocetin cofactor assay evaluates platelet aggregation in response to ristocetin and is decreased in von Willebrand disease, confirming impaired platelet adhesion. Definition: Von Willebrand disease is the most commonly inherited bleeding disorder and is caused by deficiency or dysfunction of von Willebrand factor, which mediates platelet adhesion to subendothelial collagen and stabilizes factor VIII. Prevention: Avoidance of medications that impair platelet function, such as NSAIDs, decreases bleeding risk. Treatment: Management includes desmopressin to increase release of von Willebrand factor in mild cases or factor replacement in severe disease. Differential: This patient’s presentation is consistent with a platelet adhesion disorder rather than a coagulation factor deficiency. Hemophilia A and B present with deep tissue bleeding such as hemarthroses and are caused by deficiencies of factor VIII and IX (plasma thromboplastin), respectively, rather than platelet adhesion defects. Platelet function disorders can cause mucocutaneous bleeding but are typically associated with abnormal platelet counts or medication use. Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D. Choice A: Circulating anticoagulant assay is incorrect. This evaluates for inhibitors such as lupus anticoagulant and is associated with thrombosis rather than bleeding. Choice B: Euglobulin clot lysis assay is incorrect. This assesses fibrinolysis and is not used to diagnose platelet adhesion disorders. Choice C: Factor VIII assay is incorrect. Factor VIII deficiency causes hemophilia A, which presents with hemarthroses and deep tissue bleeding, not mucocutaneous bleeding. Choice D: Factor IX assay is incorrect. Factor IX deficiency causes hemophilia B, which also presents with deep tissue bleeding rather than mucocutaneous bleeding.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine examination. During the interview, he states that he has bruises on his knees from bumping into a sofa yesterday. He has a 20-year history of easy bruising with minimal trauma. He reports bleeding profusely (approximately 1.5 cups of blood) after a dental extraction 5 years ago. He has no history of bleeding into his muscles or joints. He has no siblings, and his parents are deceased. His mother had a "bleeding problem," but the patient does not know any other details. He takes no medications. He does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol. Physical examination shows ecchymoses over the pretibial area of both lower extremities. No other abnormalities are noted. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 12.6 g/dL, a hematocrit of 37%, and a platelet count of 215,000/mm3. Which of the following is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: A. Educational Objective: This pediatric patient presents 2 weeks after allogeneic stem cell transplant with pruritic generalized erythroderma and a low-grade fever. Skin biopsy shows extensive basal layer vacuolization and multiple dyskeratotic cells, raising clinical concern for acute graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). Evaluation: Acute GVHD classically presents with involvement of the skin, gastrointestinal tract, and liver. The skin is the most frequently and earliest affected organ system and can progress from an earlier rash to diffuse, generalized erythroderma, as in this patient. Acute GVHD results from initial tissue damage followed by donor T-lymphocyte activation and expansion, which then leads to target tissue destruction. This immune-mediated process directly damages epithelial cells in the skin and can also affect epithelial tissue in the gastrointestinal tract. Definition: The gold standard for diagnosis of acute GVHD relies on clinical assessment with histopathologic confirmation. Skin biopsy is recommended to support the diagnosis when acute cutaneous GVHD is suspected. Biopsy findings may include basal layer vacuolization and dyskeratotic keratinocytes, such as in this patient. Prevention: Acute GVHD can be prevented with post-transplant immunosuppressive regimens. Regimens may include tacrolimus, cyclosporine, methotrexate, and/or mycophenolate mofetil. Treatment: Treatment for acute GVHD includes systemic corticosteroid therapy, such as with methylprednisolone, and continuation of baseline immunosuppression. Differential: The differential diagnosis for pruritic generalized erythroderma with low-grade fever after allogeneic stem cell transplant includes acute GVHD, drug rash, and infection. The skin biopsy supports acute cutaneous GVHD while negative blood cultures make infection less likely. Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E. Choice B: Leukemia cutis is incorrect. This patient recently had allogeneic stem cell transplant, making leukemia and leukemia cutis much less likely. Choice C: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is incorrect. While common in young children, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome classically presents with diffuse skin pain, erythema, superficial blistering, and desquamation. This patient’s presentation is more consistent with acute GVHD. Choice D and Choice E: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis are incorrect. These conditions would present with sloughing of the skin rather than generalized erythroderma.

wrongAnswers.B: Choice B: Leukemia cutis is incorrect. This patient recently had allogeneic stem cell transplant, making leukemia and leukemia cutis much less likely.
wrongAnswers.C: Choice C: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is incorrect. wrongAnswers.D: Choice D and Choice E: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis are incorrect. These conditions would present with sloughing of the skin rather than generalized erythroderma.
wrongAnswers.E: See the shared discussion for choice D.

questions.stem: Fifteen days after undergoing a matched related allogeneic stem cell transplant for recurrent acute lymphoblastic leukemia, a 5-year-old boy has pruritic erythroderma. It initially was present over the face, hands, and feet but has spread over the entire body. He is otherwise asymptomatic. His medications are prednisone, cyclosporine, voriconazole, granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, acyclovir, and famotidine. His temperature is 38°C (100.4°F); other vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows a diffuse dry, scaly, erythematous rash. The mucous membranes appear normal. His hemoglobin concentration is 8 g/dL, leukocyte count is 1000/mm3 (2% segmented neutrophils and 98% lymphocytes), and platelet count is 20,000/mm3. Blood cultures are negative. A skin biopsy specimen shows extensive basal vacuolization and multiple dyskeratotic cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: E. Educational Objective: This 17-year-old patient’s fever, anal pain, erythematous anus, and tender, fluctuant mass on rectal examination are suggestive of perirectal abscess. Evaluation: A perirectal abscess typically presents with fever as well as anorectal pain and swelling. Definition: Perirectal abscesses may result from obstruction of the anal glands. The condition is more likely to occur in female patients between age 20 and 40 years. Prevention: There are no established ways to prevent the development of perirectal abscesses. If a patient has an underlying condition such as Crohn disease, management of the condition may decrease the risk for abscess formation. Treatment: Treatment of a perirectal abscess includes prompt incision and drainage as well as antibiotics for those with systemic signs of infection or surrounding cellulitis. After drainage, there is a high rate of recurrence within the first year. Differential: This 17-year-old patient with severe anal pain and fever is found to have a tender, fluctuant mass on rectal examination. The most likely cause of her symptoms is a perirectal abscess. Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, and F. Choice A: Anal duct cyst is incorrect. An anal duct cyst is typically asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic without acute inflammatory features. Anal duct cysts often remain undetected for years and are only identified if they become infected or cause mass effect. Choice B: Anogenital wart is incorrect. An anogenital wart often presents as a painless, verrucous or papillomatous lesion that can be found on the external genitalia or perianal skin. Anogenital warts are caused by the human papillomavirus. Choice C: Bartholin abscess is incorrect. A Bartholin abscess occurs in the Bartholin gland, which is present at the base of the labia minora. The location of this patient’s abscess makes a perirectal abscess more likely. Choice D: Hemorrhoid is incorrect. Hemorrhoids result from dilated submucosal veins in the anal canal. They are commonly classified as either internal or external based on their relation to the pectinate line of the anal canal. Internal hemorrhoids are typically painless owing to their visceral innervation proximal to the pectinate line, while external hemorrhoids are painful because of somatic innervation distal to the pectinate line. This patient’s presentation is more consistent with a perirectal abscess. Choice F: Pilonidal cyst is incorrect. A pilonidal cyst occurs in the sacrococcygeal region of the gluteal cleft. The location of this patient’s fluctuant mass makes a perirectal abscess the most likely diagnosis.

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: E. Educational Objective: This patient most likely has leiomyomata uteri (fibroids), which commonly present with heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic pressure, and an enlarged, irregular uterus in reproductive-age women. Pelvic ultrasonography is the initial diagnostic test of choice for evaluating suspected uterine masses. Evaluation: Leiomyomata uteri typically present in reproductive-age women with menorrhagia, dysmenorrhea, pelvic fullness, and sometimes urinary frequency due to mass effect. On examination, the uterus is enlarged, mobile, and irregularly contoured, and pelvic ultrasonography is used to confirm the diagnosis. Definition: Leiomyomata uteri are benign smooth muscle tumors of the myometrium and are the most common pelvic tumors in women. They are estrogen-sensitive and typically grow during reproductive years. Depending on their size and location (submucosal, intramural, subserosal), leiomyomata uteri may cause heavy bleeding, pelvic pressure, or mass effects on adjacent organs such as the bladder. Although benign, they can significantly impact quality of life. Prevention: There is no definitive prevention, but hormonal regulation (eg, with oral contraceptives) may help limit symptom progression. Treatment: Treatment depends on symptom severity and includes conservative therapy, medical management (eg, hormonal therapy) or surgical options, such as myomectomy or hysterectomy. Minimally invasive procedures like uterine artery embolization may also be considered in cases of acute hemorrhage. Differential: In this reproductive-age woman with heavy menses, pelvic fullness, and a large irregular mobile uterine mass, leiomyomata uteri are the most likely diagnosis, and pelvic ultrasonography is the initial diagnostic test of choice. Her age and presentation are more consistent with leiomyomata uteri than with a uterine malignancy. Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D. Choice A: CT scan of the pelvis is incorrect. CT scan is not the first-line imaging modality for evaluating suspected uterine masses. Ultrasonography is more sensitive, cost-effective, and avoids radiation. Choice B: Hysteroscopy is incorrect. Hysteroscopy is useful for evaluating intrauterine pathology (eg, submucosal fibroids or polyps) but is not the initial diagnostic test for a large pelvic mass. Choice C: Measurement of serum CA 125 concentration is incorrect. Serum CA 125 concentration may be increased in ovarian cancer but is nonspecific and not appropriate for initial evaluation of suspected leiomyomata uteri. Choice D: Operative exploration is incorrect. Surgery is not indicated before establishing a diagnosis with noninvasive imaging, such as ultrasonography.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, comes to the physician because of a 1-year history of moderate menstrual pain and heavy flow. During this time, she also has had pelvic fullness and mild urinary urgency. Menses occur at regular 26-day intervals and last 7 days. She has hypertension treated with lisinopril. She does not appear to be in distress. Vital signs are within normal limits. The abdomen is soft and nontender. Pelvic examination shows a 16-cm, nontender, mobile, midline pelvic mass with irregular contour. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices: Measurement of serum creatine kinase activity
questions.explanation: Correct Answer: A. Educational Objective: The most appropriate next step for this patient is determination of urine albumin:creatinine ratio. Patients with diabetes mellitus require annual screening for diabetic nephropathy with a urine albumin:creatinine ratio, even when glycemic control appears adequate. Evaluation: This patient has well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus with appropriate prior screening for retinopathy and neuropathy but no documented recent evaluation for nephropathy, which is a key component of routine surveillance. Definition: Diabetic nephropathy is characterized by progressive albuminuria due to glomerular hyperfiltration and damage to the glomerular basement membrane. Screening is performed using a spot urine albumin:creatinine ratio, which detects microalbuminuria, defined as 30 to 300 mg/g. Guidelines recommend annual screening beginning at diagnosis in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus because disease onset often precedes diagnosis. Early detection allows for interventions such as ACE inhibitor therapy or angiotensin II receptor blocker therapy to slow progression to chronic kidney disease. Prevention: Tight glycemic and blood pressure control decreases the risk for developing diabetic nephropathy. Treatment: Initiation or optimization of ACE inhibitor therapy or angiotensin II receptor blocker therapy is indicated in patients with albuminuria. Differential: Diabetic retinopathy and neuropathy are other microvascular complications, but this patient has already been appropriately screened for these. Dyslipidemia is present but is already being treated and does not change immediate management. Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E. Choice B: Measurement of serum creatine kinase activity is incorrect. This is used to evaluate statin-associated myopathy and is not indicated without muscle symptoms. Choice C: Measurement of serum transaminase activities is incorrect. Routine monitoring of transaminases is not required in asymptomatic patients on statins with no risk factors or symptoms of hepatotoxicity. Choice D: Measurement of urine glucose concentration is incorrect. This does not provide useful information for diabetes mellitus management or complication screening. Choice E: Oral glucose tolerance test is incorrect. This is used for diagnosis of diabetes mellitus, not for monitoring or complication screening in an established patient.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and hyperlipidemia comes to the physician for a routine examination. He reports that he feels well and has seen no abnormalities during his daily foot checking. His medications are metformin and simvastatin. During the past 3 months, his fingerstick blood glucose concentrations have ranged between 110 mg/dL and 150 mg/dL. An annual funduscopic examination 2 months ago showed no abnormalities. Six months ago, he received the influenza virus vaccine. Three years ago, he received the tetanus-diphtheria-acellular pertussis and pneumococcal vaccines. He follows a healthy diet and exercises for 30 minutes four times weekly. He is 183 cm (6 ft) tall and weighs 91 kg (200 lb); BMI is 27 kg/m2. His pulse is 55/min, and blood pressure is 122/72 mm Hg. Examination, including monofilament testing, shows no other abnormalities. His hemoglobin A1c 6 months ago was 6.4%. Laboratory studies today show: Hemoglobin A1c 6.8% Serum Cholesterol, total 153 mg/dL HDL-cholesterol 43 mg/dL LDL-cholesterol 70 mg/dL Triglycerides 199 mg/dL Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: D. Educational Objective: This patient presents with a 1-week history of foul-smelling, nonbloody, and floating diarrhea. The most likely causal organism is Giardia lamblia. Evaluation: Giardiasis presents with persistent diarrhea that is foul-smelling and fatty, as well as abdominal pain, bloating, cramping, and weight loss. Definition: G lamblia is a flagellated, parasitic organism that causes giardiasis. Parasitic overgrowth of the small bowel leads to the intestinal malabsorption of fats and carbohydrates. Children and infants are more likely than adults to present with dehydration and may experience failure to thrive as a result of malnutrition secondary to malabsorption. Diagnosis is made with stool culture, microscopy, or stool antigen testing. Prevention: Giardiasis is usually acquired through the ingestion of cysts in contaminated water, which then mature into trophozoites in the small bowel. Treatment: Giardiasis is typically treated with antimicrobial agents. The most commonly used include metronidazole, tinidazole, and nitazoxanide. Differential: This patient who works in a day-care center presents with foul-smelling and floating diarrhea. G lamblia is the most likely causal organism. The other organisms listed would be more likely to present with watery or bloody diarrhea. Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E. Choice A: Clostridioides difficile is incorrect. C difficile is an opportunistic and often hospital-acquired infection that commonly occurs after the use of antibiotics due to the loss of native colonic microbiota that allows competition-free proliferation of C difficile. Patients typically present with watery diarrhea and abdominal pain. This patient’s presentation is most consistent with G lamblia as the most likely causal organism. Choice B: Cryptosporidium parvum is incorrect. C parvum is a parasitic infection that causes cryptosporidiosis. Infection is characterized by watery diarrhea and more commonly affects immunocompromised hosts. Choice C: Escherichia coli is incorrect. E coli can be enterotoxigenic or enterohemorrhagic, presenting with either watery or bloody diarrhea, respectively. This patient’s foul-smelling and floating stools make G lamblia more likely. Choice E: Yersinia enterocolitica is incorrect. Y enterocolitica is a gram-negative rod that causes bloody diarrhea and abdominal pain. It results as a consequence of consuming contaminated food or water.

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: B. Educational Objective: This patient presents with constant, sharp, severe right-sided back pain that radiates to the right groin, and calcifications over the right renal fossa are shown on abdominal x-ray. The most likely diagnosis is nephrolithiasis. Evaluation: Nephrolithiasis may present with severe, intermittent, sharp flank pain; leukocytosis, with or without gross or microscopic hematuria; and possible evidence of a concomitant urinary tract infection. Definition: Nephrolithiasis and ureterolithiasis describe the formation or presence of calculi within the urinary collecting system, commonly known as kidney stones or ureteral stones. Calcium-containing stones are the most common varieties, although kidney stones may also be composed of cystine, struvite, or uric acid. CT scan of the abdomen without contrast is a sensitive modality for the detection of kidney stones as it can identify both radiopaque and radiolucent stones. Prevention: Nephrolithiasis may be prevented with adequate hydration and dietary changes. Treatment: Acute management depends on the size and location of the stone in addition to complicating factors such as abnormal anatomy or the concurrent presence of a urinary tract infection. Stones larger than 6 mm often require intervention as they are unlikely to pass on their own. Differential: This patient presents with acute right-sided back pain that radiates to the right groin. In addition, she is found to have hematuria on urinalysis as well as calcifications over the right renal fossa on abdominal x-ray. These findings make nephrolithiasis the most likely diagnosis. Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E. Choice A: Biliary colic is incorrect. Biliary colic, which is characterized by intense, short-lasting right upper quadrant abdominal pain associated with nausea and vomiting after heavy meals, is commonly caused by cholelithiasis. Cholelithiasis may be associated with acute cholecystitis, ascending cholangitis, or acute pancreatitis. Choice C: Pyelonephritis is incorrect. Pyelonephritis is a urinary tract infection that has spread to the kidneys. This is characterized by flank pain, fever and chills, nausea, vomiting, and costovertebral tenderness on physical examination. Choice D: Spontaneous renal hemorrhage is incorrect. Spontaneous renal hemorrhage most commonly presents with a tender palpable mass and signs of hypovolemia or shock. Nephrolithiasis is more likely in this case. Choice E: Urinary tract infection is incorrect. Urinary tract infections classically present in female patients with dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency, and suprapubic discomfort. They are often caused by Escherichia coli or other gram-negative enteric flora.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-hour history of severe right-sided back pain. The pain is constant and sharp and radiates to her right groin. She also has had dull, aching, right-sided abdominal pain during this time. She is nauseated and has vomited once. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 34/min, and blood pressure is 108/62 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 94%. Breath sounds are slightly decreased at the right lung base. Abdominal examination shows right-sided tenderness to palpation; bowel sounds are decreased. On urinalysis, RBCs are too numerous to count. A Gram stain of urine shows few gram-negative rods. Abdominal x-ray shows a nonspecific gas pattern with calcifications over the right renal fossa. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: D. Educational Objective: Posttest probability is the probability of the patient having the disease after receiving the results of a test. Posttest probability is calculated as pretest probability × likelihood ratio, which in this case is 10% × 6.6, or 66%. Key Concept: The sensitivity, specificity, and likelihood ratios of a test are fixed values inherent to the test. In contrast, pretest and posttest probability are influenced by individual and clinical factors in addition to the characteristics of the test. Explanation: Pretest probability is the probability of the patient having the disease prior to undergoing the test (in this vignette, estimated by the physician to be 10%). It is often equated to the prevalence of the disease in the population; however, in practice, this can increase or decrease based on data from prior tests and clinical judgment. Posttest probability is the probability of the patient having the disease after receiving test results. Differential: Posttest probability = pretest probability × likelihood ratio. When applied to this patient, this results in a posttest probability of 66%. 73% represents posttest odds, while the other options represent incorrect numbers/calculations. Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E. Choices A, B, and C: 34%, 42%, and 59% are incorrect. These answer choices represent erroneous calculations or the use of random, incorrect numbers that do not represent the appropriate calculation of the posttest probability or other epidemiologic measures. Choice E: 73% is incorrect. This is the posttest odds, not the posttest probability.

questions.stem: A 2-month-old boy is being evaluated for developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) using a standardized screening protocol that has a positive likelihood ratio of 6.6 and a negative likelihood ratio of 0.1. Prior to beginning the screening protocol, the physician estimates that the patient’s probability of having DDH is 10%. Results of the screening protocol are positive. Based on the results of the screening protocol, which of the following is the post-test probability that this patient has DDH?

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: D. Educational Objective: Deep venous thrombosis (DVT) is a common complication in pregnancy due to physiologic changes that increase venous stasis and hypercoagulability. The most appropriate treatment in this pregnant patient with confirmed DVT is subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) therapy to prevent further clot extension and decrease the risk for pulmonary embolism (PE). Evaluation: DVT during pregnancy classically presents with unilateral leg pain, swelling, and erythema, often in the second or third trimester, but can also occur in early pregnancy. Venous duplex ultrasonography is the gold standard for diagnosis, as it accurately detects the presence of a thrombus in the deep veins. Definition: Pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state due to increased concentrations of clotting factors, venous stasis, and decreased fibrinolysis. These changes make pregnant patients particularly susceptible to venous thromboembolism (VTE), including DVT and PE. This patient's presentation with unilateral leg swelling and pain, along with the confirmed DVT on venous duplex ultrasonography, is classic for pregnancy-related DVT. Prevention: Prevention of VTE during pregnancy involves early mobilization, use of compression stockings, and in some cases, prophylactic anticoagulation, particularly in high-risk individuals such as those with a prior history of VTE or genetic predisposition to clot formation. Treatment: In a pregnant patient with DVT, the most appropriate treatment is subcutaneous LMWH therapy, which should be continued until delivery. LMWH therapy is preferred due to its safety profile in pregnancy. Postpartum anticoagulation may continue depending on the patient's risk for bleeding and clot recurrence. Differential: This pregnant patient with a confirmed DVT is at risk for VTE because of the hypercoagulable state of pregnancy. LMWH therapy is the treatment of choice for DVT during pregnancy. Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E. Choice A: Intravenous tissue plasminogen activator therapy is incorrect. Thrombolytic therapy with tissue plasminogen activator is typically reserved for massive or life-threatening thromboembolic events such as acute PE with hemodynamic instability, acute ischemic stroke, or myocardial infarction if catheterization cannot occur within 120 minutes. Tissue plasminogen activator therapy is not indicated for the management of uncomplicated DVT, particularly in pregnancy. Choice B: Oral direct thrombin inhibitor therapy is incorrect. Direct thrombin inhibitors (eg, dabigatran) are not recommended in pregnancy due to insufficient safety data. LMWH is the preferred anticoagulant for DVT management in pregnancy. Choice C: Placement of a vena cava filter is incorrect. A vena cava filter is typically used in patients with a contraindication to anticoagulation or in those with recurrent PE despite adequate anticoagulation. This patient has no contraindication to anticoagulation and is a candidate for LMWH therapy. Choice E: Surgical vena cava ligation is incorrect. Surgical vena cava ligation is an outdated and rarely used procedure. It is not indicated for the treatment of DVT, as current management relies on anticoagulation therapy to prevent further clot formation and complications such as PE.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, at 12 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of the sudden onset of pain in her left thigh and swelling of her left leg. Her previous pregnancies and spontaneous vaginal deliveries were uncomplicated and at term. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 118/76 mm Hg. On examination, peripheral pulses are 2+. Capillary refill time of the left lower extremity is less than 1 second. There is 2+ pitting edema of the left lower extremity. Venous duplex ultrasonography shows a clot extending from the popliteal to the femoral vein. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices: CT angiography of the right lower extremity
Digital subtraction angiography of the right lower extremity
Duplex ultrasonography of the right lower extremity
Surgical exploration of the right thigh hematoma
questions.explanation: Correct Answer: E. Educational Objective: This patient presents with an active hematoma in the medial right thigh and hemodynamic instability responsive to fluids, consistent with hemorrhagic shock from femoral artery injury. The most appropriate next step is immediate surgical exploration of the right thigh hematoma with surgical hemostasis. Evaluation: Hemorrhagic shock from femoral artery injury classically presents with tachycardia, hypotension, and visible or concealed thigh hemorrhage. The gold standard for diagnosis of femoral artery injury in a clinically stable patient is CT angiography of the thigh. However, in the setting of hemodynamic instability, CT angiography should be deferred in favor of immediate surgical exploration. The proximal thigh can conceal large volumes of blood, making concealed hemorrhage a possibility. Patients who present with hypotension that is fluid responsive likely have ongoing bleeding and are at risk of death from hemorrhagic shock. Definition: Hemorrhagic shock from femoral artery injury results from a laceration or puncture injury of the femoral artery, resulting in massive, rapid blood loss. It is a life-threatening medical emergency requiring immediate surgical exploration and hemostasis. Prevention: Hemorrhagic shock can be prevented by immediate tourniquet application proximal to the site of hemorrhage. When the injury is close to the groin, hemorrhage control may require a hemostatic dressing or manual compression while preparing for surgical exploration. Treatment: Treatment for hemorrhagic shock in the setting of traumatic thigh injury includes resuscitation with hemorrhage control and blood product transfusion, along with immediate surgical exploration when there are signs of vascular injury. Differential: This patient's differential includes hemorrhagic shock from femoral artery injury, which is the most likely diagnosis, as well as traumatic femoral vein injury with significant blood loss and polytrauma. Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D. Choice A: CT angiography of the right lower extremity is incorrect. While CT angiography is the preferred diagnostic test in a stable patient, this patient is hemodynamically unstable and may not have time to undergo imaging. Immediate surgical exploration is the more appropriate next step. Choice B: Digital subtraction angiography of the right lower extremity is incorrect. While digital subtraction angiography may characterize vascular damage, this patient is decompensating and requires immediate surgical exploration rather than further imaging. Choice C: Duplex ultrasonography of the right lower extremity is incorrect. The clinical concern is not for venous thrombosis, and this patient requires operative hemorrhage control rather than imaging. Choice D: Exploratory laparotomy is incorrect. While this patient requires surgery, the indicated procedure is surgical exploration of the right thigh hematoma, not abdominal exploration.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by paramedics 25 minutes after he was stabbed in the right thigh. He says he has severe pain in the right lower extremity. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He drinks three 12-oz beers and smokes marijuana daily. His pulse is 110/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 90/50 mm Hg. Examination shows a large hematoma in the medial aspect of the right thigh near the groin; there is no pulsatile bleeding. The right foot is cool to the touch. Right dorsalis pedis and posterior tibialis pulses are absent. Motor examination of the right foot shows no abnormalities. Sensation to touch over the right foot is intact. Infusion of 2 L of lactated Ringer solution is begun. Five minutes later, his blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices: Measurement of serum follicle-stimulating hormone concentration
Ten-day course of oral progesterone therapy
questions.explanation: Correct Answer: B. Educational Objective: Primary amenorrhea evaluation depends on age and pubertal development, with investigation typically indicated in patients aged older than 15 years or more than 3 years after thelarche. Adolescent patients such as this one with normal secondary sex characteristics who have not yet reached these thresholds can be managed with observation and follow-up. Key Concept: This 15-year-old patient has primary amenorrhea but began breast development at age 14 years. Menarche normally occurs within 2 to 3 years after thelarche, so her presentation falls within the expected developmental window and does not yet require evaluation or treatment. Explanation: Primary amenorrhea is defined as the absence of menarche by age 15 years or within 3 years of breast development. The timing of puberty follows a predictable sequence: thelarche, pubarche, then menarche. In patients with normal secondary sex characteristics, the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis is functioning, suggesting that delayed menarche may still be physiologic. Common causes of primary amenorrhea differ depending on the presence or absence of secondary sex characteristics and include outflow tract abnormalities, gonadal dysgenesis, or endocrine disorders. However, early in pubertal development, watchful waiting is appropriate if progression is otherwise normal. Differential: In this 15-year-old patient with normal pubertal development who presents only 1 year since thelarche, physiologic delay is most likely. Immediate diagnostic testing is unnecessary unless she reaches 3 years post-thelarche, passes 16 years old, or develops other abnormalities. Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E. Choice A: CT scan of the head is incorrect. CT scan of the head is incorrect because there are no signs of central nervous system pathology (eg, headaches, visual changes, delayed puberty without breast development) to suggest a hypothalamic or pituitary lesion. Choice C: Measurement of serum follicle-stimulating hormone concentration is incorrect. Hormonal evaluation is premature in a patient who is still within the normal window for menarche after thelarche. Choice D: Ten-day course of oral progesterone therapy is incorrect. Progesterone challenges are used to evaluate secondary amenorrhea or established primary amenorrhea after appropriate timing thresholds have been met, which is not the case with this patient. Choice E: Vaginal ultrasonography is incorrect. Vaginal ultrasonography is used to evaluate structural causes of amenorrhea such as gonadal dysgenesis, imperforate hymen, or uterine septations. Structural evaluation is not indicated in this patient whose development otherwise appears normal.

The patient has no history of serious illness and has never been sexually active. She takes no medications. She is 160 cm (5 ft 3 in) tall and weighs 50 kg (110 lb); BMI is 20 kg/m2. questions.explanation: Correct Answer: D. Educational Objective: Herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE) is most commonly caused by infection with herpes simplex virus type 1 and typically presents with acute fever, altered mental status, abnormal behavior, and focal neurologic symptoms. No established postexposure prophylaxis regimen for herpes simplex virus type 1 exists. This patient’s close contacts should follow standard precautions to decrease risk for transmission through safe practices, but no prophylaxis is indicated. Evaluation: Patients with HSE often present with acute fever, headache, altered mental status, abnormal behavior, and focal neurologic deficits (eg, seizure, aphasia, hemiparesis, cranial nerve deficits). The temporal lobe is frequently affected. Definition: HSE is a severe viral infection of the central nervous system caused predominantly by herpes simplex virus type 1. Less than 10% of HSE cases are caused by herpes simplex virus type 2, which occurs primarily in newborns and immunocompromised patients. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis in the setting of HSE typically shows increased opening pressure, increased leukocyte count with lymphocytic predominance, as well as increased protein concentration and normal glucose concentration. Red blood cells may be present due to temporal hemorrhage. MRI of the brain often shows abnormalities in the temporal lobes, which can include edema, hemorrhage, and necrosis. Prevention: Prevention of HSE focuses on decreasing the risk for herpesvirus infection through safe practices (eg, not sharing drinks and abstaining from sex during outbreaks), and awareness can help prevent the occurrence of HSE. There is otherwise no specific preventive measure or recommended postexposure prophylaxis. Treatment: Intravenous acyclovir is the primary treatment, initiated as soon as HSE is suspected. Supportive care for seizures and increased intracranial pressure may be indicated. Even with prompt diagnosis and treatment, mortality is high and patients are at risk for long-term neuropsychiatric morbidity. Differential: This patient’s acute headache, fever, meningismus, confusion, and focal neurologic deficits are most suggestive of meningitis or encephalitis. Her CSF analysis findings are consistent with a viral cause, and temporal lobe changes with CSF erythrocytes point to a herpesvirus infection, the most common cause of infectious encephalitis. No effective postexposure prophylaxis exists for herpesvirus infection, so prophylaxis is not indicated for this patient’s recent contacts. Incorrect Answers: A, B, and C. Choice A: Only the physician who performed the patient’s lumbar puncture is incorrect. Standard sterile practices while performing lumbar puncture include wearing masks and gloves, which are sufficient to avoid transmission of herpesvirus. Transmission via exposure to CSF is theoretically possible in cases of Ebola meningoencephalitis; however, this is rare and this patient has no history of recent travel to endemic areas. Choice B: People who had contact with the patient’s mucous membranes or broken skin is incorrect. Prophylaxis for these contacts is indicated when there is concern for rabies or uncommon zoonotic encephalitides such as cercopithecine herpesvirus 1 (B virus). Choice C: People who had contact with the patient’s respiratory secretions is incorrect. Prophylaxis for individuals exposed to a patient’s respiratory secretions is indicated in cases of specific pathogens that spread easily person-to-person such as Haemophilus influenzae and Neisseria meningitidis.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of moderate headache and neck stiffness and a 3-hour history of confusion. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol. On arrival, she is awake. Her temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 130/78 mm Hg. Cranial nerve and motor examinations show no abnormalities. Deep tendon reflexes are 3+ and symmetric. Babinski sign is present bilaterally. Sensation is intact. On mental status examination, she is oriented to person but not to place or time. questions.explanation: Correct Answer: C. Educational Objective: This patient presents with chronic disorganized thought process, laughing to himself (reflecting internal stimulation by hallucinations), and social withdrawal (representing a prodromal period and/or apathy). This presentation is consistent with schizophrenia. Evaluation: Patients with schizophrenia demonstrate at least two of the following five symptoms: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior, or negative symptoms (eg, flat affect, apathy, alogia). Negative symptoms may also manifest as poor personal hygiene. Many patients also demonstrate prodromal periods of strange behavior and decreased functioning. The total duration of symptoms must exceed 6 months and affect daily functionality to meet diagnostic criteria. Definition: The cause of schizophrenia is thought to include dopamine dysregulation, and brain imaging typically shows decreased cortical volume and enlarged ventricles. A family history of bipolar disorder or schizophrenia is common. Prevention: Though there is no universal way to prevent schizophrenia, avoiding cannabis use during adolescence (especially in patients with a family history of serious mental illness) is likely beneficial for decreasing future schizophrenia risk. Treatment: Treatment of schizophrenia requires antipsychotics, which can be divided into two groups: typical (haloperidol, fluphenazine, chlorpromazine) and atypical (risperidone, aripiprazole, olanzapine). Differential: A substance-induced psychotic disorder (eg, stimulant-induced psychotic disorder or cannabis-induced psychotic disorder) should be excluded. Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E. Choice A: Autism spectrum disorder is incorrect. Patients with autism spectrum disorder typically present with deficits in social communication and restricted interests from early childhood. This patient’s symptoms started in his teenage years. Though patients with schizophrenia commonly demonstrate impaired social communication, they also typically present with hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized thinking. Choice B: Schizoaffective disorder is incorrect. Patients with schizoaffective disorder demonstrate psychotic symptoms along with significant mood episodes (eg, major depressive episodes, manic episodes). Though this patient appears sad, he does not report other depressive symptoms (eg, energy or appetite changes) consistent with a major depressive episode. His social withdrawal appears related to internal stimulation by hallucinations and apathy rather than anhedonia or decreased motivation. Choice D: Sexual abuse is incorrect. Though patients who have experienced abuse commonly exhibit fear and easy startle, as in this patient, psychotic symptoms and negative symptoms (eg, apathy) are atypical. Choice E: Substance-induced mood disorder is incorrect. This patient’s urine toxicology screening was negative, and this patient demonstrates psychotic symptoms rather than mood symptoms.

He spends a lot of time in his room alone; when his mother checks on him, she hears laughter. His appetite and energy level are unchanged. He says that he is spending several hours each day on his homework, but his grades have steadily declined during the past 5 months. There have been no recent stressors in his life. On examination, he has a sad affect. He is apprehensive, looking around the room at the slightest hallway noise. His eye contact is furtive, and he is unable to provide coherent answers to the physician's questions. Results of laboratory studies are within the reference ranges. Urine toxicology screening is negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: A. Educational Objective: For this young, tall patient who presents with shortness of breath, a grade 2/6 diastolic murmur at the mid left sternal border, and a blood pressure of 140/58 mm Hg indicating a wide pulse pressure, the most likely diagnosis is aortic regurgitation. One of the more common causes of aortic regurgitation in young athletes is a connective tissue disorder leading to aortic root dilation and subsequent aortic regurgitation. Evaluation: Aortic regurgitation classically presents as a diagnosis made incidentally on physical examination. However, as patients decompensate, they can develop ongoing shortness of breath and pulmonary edema consistent with heart failure. On auscultation, aortic regurgitation produces a blowing early diastolic decrescendo murmur best heard at the left sternal border. The gold standard for diagnosis of aortic regurgitation is echocardiography. Definition: Aortic regurgitation results from backward flow of blood from the aorta into the left ventricle during diastole due to incomplete closure of the aortic valve, causing increased volume and pressure overload on the left ventricle and potentially leading to ventricular dysfunction if untreated. Prevention: There is no specific prevention for aortic regurgitation. However, early identification and management of underlying conditions is crucial. For patients with diagnosed connective tissue disorders, annual echocardiographic surveillance of their valvular disease is recommended. Treatment: Treatment for aortic regurgitation includes medical optimization and, in qualifying patients, surgical aortic valve replacement. Differential: This patient's differential diagnosis is initially broad given that he is an athlete who presents with shortness of breath. However, his tall stature and thin build raise concern for a connective tissue disorder such as Marfan syndrome as the cause of his aortic regurgitation. A grade 2/6 diastolic murmur at the mid left sternal border is most consistent with aortic regurgitation, and the wide pulse pressure further supports this diagnosis. Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, E, F, and G. Choice B: Aortic stenosis is incorrect. Aortic stenosis produces a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur, not a diastolic murmur as heard in this patient. Choice C: Coarctation of the aorta is incorrect. Coarctation of the aorta produces a systolic murmur and would not account for the diastolic murmur heard in this patient. Choice D: Flow murmur is incorrect. Flow murmurs are more commonly heard in pediatric patients and do not contribute to the development of heart failure symptoms. Choice E: Mitral regurgitation is incorrect. Mitral regurgitation produces a holosystolic murmur, not a diastolic murmur. Choice F: Mitral stenosis is incorrect. While mitral stenosis can produce a diastolic murmur, this patient's wide pulse pressure, indicated by a blood pressure of 140/58 mm Hg, is more consistent with aortic regurgitation than mitral stenosis. Choice G: Patent ductus arteriosus is incorrect. Patent ductus arteriosus produces a continuous machine-like murmur and would be an unlikely diagnosis in a 21-year-old man.

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: B. Educational Objective: Intravenous administration of calcium chloride is the most appropriate next step in treatment for this patient. Severe hyperkalemia with ECG changes requires immediate cardiac membrane stabilization with intravenous calcium. Evaluation: This patient who missed dialysis presents with severe hyperkalemia and ECG changes, placing him at high risk for life-threatening arrhythmias. Definition: Hyperkalemia is defined as serum potassium greater than 5.0 mEq/L and becomes life-threatening at concentrations greater than approximately 6.5 mEq/L, especially when ECG changes are present. Characteristic findings include peaked T waves, widened QRS complexes, and eventual progression to ventricular arrhythmias. In patients with renal failure, impaired potassium excretion leads to accumulation. The immediate priority in management is stabilization of the cardiac membrane with intravenous calcium, which does not decrease potassium but decreases the risk for arrhythmias. Subsequent therapies shift potassium intracellularly or remove it from the body. Prevention: Adherence to dialysis schedules and avoidance of potassium-retaining medications decrease risk for hyperkalemia. Treatment: Treatment of severe hyperkalemia includes immediate intravenous calcium followed by measures to decrease serum potassium, including insulin with glucose, β-adrenergic agonists, and dialysis. Differential: Volume overload can cause dyspnea and crackles but would not explain ECG changes associated with hyperkalemia. Uremia causes systemic symptoms but is not responsible for acute arrhythmogenic risk. Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, E, and F. Choice A: Atenolol is incorrect. β-Adrenergic blockers can worsen hyperkalemia by decreasing cellular potassium uptake. Choice C: Furosemide is incorrect. Loop diuretics promote potassium excretion but are ineffective in anuric renal failure. Choice D: Lidocaine is incorrect. Lidocaine is an antiarrhythmic but does not treat the underlying electrolyte abnormality. Choice E: Magnesium sulfate is incorrect. Magnesium sulfate is used for treatment of torsades de pointes, not hyperkalemia. Choice F: 0.9% Saline is incorrect. Fluid administration does not correct hyperkalemia and may worsen volume overload in renal failure.

choiceHtml: Ask the patient to borrow money for the nutritionist visits
Explain to the insurance agent that the patient meets criteria for diabetes mellitus
File a formal appeal with the patient’s insurance company
Wait for the patient’s fasting serum glucose concentration to increase and then refer him again to the nutritionist

File a formal appeal with the patient’s insurance company

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: C. Educational Objective: Physicians should advocate for patients to receive appropriate, medically necessary care, even when insurance coverage is initially denied. Filing a formal appeal is an appropriate and ethical step when evidence-based interventions are indicated but not covered. Key Concept: Patient advocacy includes working within healthcare systems to overcome barriers to care, including insurance limitations. Explanation: This patient has prediabetes (hemoglobin A1c 6%, fasting glucose 119 mg/dL), obesity, and significant lifestyle risk factors, making nutritional counseling medically appropriate to prevent progression to diabetes mellitus. Although his insurance does not routinely cover nutritionist visits for prediabetes, the physician still has a responsibility to advocate for necessary preventive care. The most appropriate next step is to file a formal appeal with the insurance company providing clinical justification for why the service is needed. This approach maintains honesty while attempting to secure appropriate care for the patient. It aligns with ethical principles of beneficence and justice by promoting access to preventive interventions. Differential: The physician in this case has a responsibility to advocate for appropriate access to preventive care to prevent disease progression in this patient. The patient’s age and metabolic risk profile indicate prediabetes rather than overt diabetes mellitus, so explaining to the insurance agent that the patient meets the criteria is false and inappropriate. The correct action balances ethical integrity with advocacy by pursuing formal channels rather than misrepresentation or inaction. Incorrect Answers: A, B, and D. Choice A: Ask the patient to borrow money for the nutritionist visits is incorrect. This places an inappropriate financial burden on the patient without first attempting system-level solutions. Physicians should advocate for coverage before suggesting out-of-pocket payment. Choice B: Explain to the insurance agent that the patient meets criteria for diabetes mellitus is incorrect. This is factually incorrect and constitutes dishonest representation/fraud. The patient has prediabetes, not diabetes mellitus, and falsifying information is unethical and illegal. Choice D: Wait for the patient’s fasting serum glucose concentration to increase and then refer him again to the nutritionist is incorrect. Deliberately delaying preventive care until the patient develops a more serious condition is harmful. Early intervention is key in preventing progression to diabetes mellitus.

questions.explanation: Correct Answer: A. Educational Objective: The pearly papule on this patient’s nose is a basal cell carcinoma. The most likely clinical course is complete resolution following resection of the skin cancer. Evaluation: Basal cell carcinoma presents clinically as a pearly papule with rolled borders, overlying telangiectasia, and may be eroded or ulcerated. Patients often describe basal cell carcinoma as “the pimple that will not pop” or “wound that will not heal.” Basal cell carcinoma is locally invasive, and distant metastasis is extremely rare. Definition: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common form of skin cancer and is associated with UV light exposure and mutations in PTCH1. Basal cell carcinoma pathology shows islands of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and retraction from the surrounding dermis. Prevention: Avoidance of prolonged UV light exposure may prevent development of basal cell carcinoma. Treatment: The preferred treatment of basal cell carcinoma on high-risk areas, such as the nose, is Mohs micrographic surgery. Other treatments include surgical excision, electrodesiccation and curettage, topical imiquimod therapy, and radiation therapy. Differential: For this patient with a painless, pearly papule of the nose, the most likely diagnosis is basal cell carcinoma, which shows resolution following complete resection. Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E. Choice B: Local recurrence within 1 year is incorrect. Basal cell carcinoma shows a contiguous growth pattern; therefore, surgical removal with Mohs micrographic surgery or surgical excision has a high cure rate. Choice C and Choice D: Metastasis to bone and metastasis to the liver are incorrect. It is extremely unlikely that this superficial basal cell carcinoma of the nose would metastasize to the bone or the liver. Bone metastasis is more common in long-standing, large basal cell carcinomas. Additionally, metastasis to the liver or other solid organs is very rare for basal cell carcinoma. Choice E: Ulceration at the biopsy site is incorrect. Following resection, the most likely scenario is complete resolution. Ulceration of a previously treated basal cell carcinoma scar is suggestive of tumor recurrence.
